summary: Intro demo covering hosted chat/textgen basics with emphasis on streaming response shape, parameter tuning for latency vs cost, retry patterns and a tour of the Console Optimize suggestions. Customer: BlueHarbor Logistics exploring a pilot to augment customer support triage and real-time ETA generation.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — really appreciate you squeezing this in. Quick roll call?
[00:05] Priya (Head of Product): Hi yes Priya here, Ethan on shortly, Carlos is on.
[00:10] Ethan (Platform Eng): Hey sorry for being two minutes late, Ethan here.
[00:18] Maya: Awesome. The agenda — very pragmatic: 1) live demo of our Hosted API chat/text generation streaming, 2) Console tour (models, routing, rollouts), 3) Optimize suggestions for cost/latency, and 4) Q&A + next steps. We'll try to keep to 45 min with time for questions.
[00:35] Carlos (CTO): Sounds good. We're mostly curious about real-time latencies and how retries look in practice.
[00:42] Liam (SE): Great, I'll share my screen for a short sandbox. Just call out if you want a different prompt set.
[00:48] [Liam shares sandbox console link: https://redwood.example/sandbox/blueharbor]
[00:55] Liam: So first bit, streaming. Redwood streams tokens as they're generated — we send a continuous chunked response. Common question: how big is each chunk? It depends on model and tokenizer — typically 10-50 bytes per frame for English prose, but if you do structured JSON outputs you'll see larger frames because of punctuation.
[01:20] Priya: Ok and how does that affect front-end rendering? We need sub-200ms perceived latency for ETA updates.
[01:28] Liam: Right, perceived latency is both first-byte and token rate. We set the model and 'max_tokens' and also use a 'response_time_threshold' in the Console to prefer lower-latency variants. For ETA you probably want a smaller max_tokens and maybe use a shorter-context prompt. That reduces time-to-first-byte. Also we have continuous prefix caching for repeated instructions which can shave off 20-30% for repeated queries.
[01:55] Ethan: Caching — is that safe for PII? We have regulated fields in our prompts.
[02:02] Maya: Good call. We can disable prefix caching per route and we support not persisting request content to logs. Also KMS-integrated encryption at rest. We'll share the security notes.
[02:20] Liam: Demo time — sending a sample triage prompt. Streaming response coming in...
[02:27] [stream begins]
[02:30] Speaker (model): "Sure, here's a short triage summary: 1) probable cause network delay, 2) suggested next step: restart modem, 3) estimated ETA: 12-18 minutes."
[02:45] Priya: That looks nice. I noticed you framed it as bullets. Are there options for structured outputs? We need machine-readable fields.
[02:53] Liam: Yup — function-style outputs or json_schema in the call. We can strongly encourage structured JSON via the prompt or use the structured output param, reminding that strict JSON can increase latency slightly since model tries to satisfy a schema.
[03:10] Carlos: Any limits on streaming length or idle timeouts?
[03:15] Liam: Idle timeout defaults to 30s on the hosted API but is configurable at the route level. If the model stalls we send a final 'incomplete' event and you can decide to retry or return partial.
[03:30] Priya: Let's talk retries — we want safe retries without duplicating side-effects.
[03:35] Liam: We recommend idempotency keys for any request that results in a persistent side-effect. For pure read/generation workloads you can do automatic retry on 5xx with exponential backoff, jittered. For streaming specifically we have a resume token approach in the Console for some models — it depends on whether model supports deterministic continuation. In practice, if you need exactly-once semantics, do idempotency keys and store the last committed response on your side.
[04:05] Ethan: For our use case we call the model, then call downstream services to update ETAs, so we need to avoid double-notifying. Idempotency sounds good. How long are keys persisted?
[04:16] Maya: Keys can be looked up for 72 hours by default — that's configurable for Dedicated/Private.
[04:22] [00:04:22 — Liam opens Console]
[04:25] Liam: Quick Console tour: here's model pinning — you can pin to a specific model version for a route and then set a canary rollout to 5% traffic to validate. Notice the routing policy options — latency-first, cost-first, or regional.
[04:40] Priya: The regional routing — can we pin US traffic to our US-only data plane? We have GDPR-ish concerns in EU.
[04:48] Liam: Yes, routing by region + data residency is supported on Private/Dedicated; hosted routes can be region-limited to a subset of regions offered. We also surface per-token cost in the Console so you can watch unit economics.
[05:05] Carlos: The Optimize tab — what does it recommend?
[05:10] Liam: Optimize looks at your route traffic and suggests batching thresholds, cache TTLs, and quantization profiles. For example, for a low-latency single-turn chat you may not want aggressive batching — Optimize will recommend small batch sizes and a low-latency kernel. For throughput-heavy background embeddings, it might recommend larger batches and an int8 quantization.
[05:33] Priya: Do those suggestions generate a config we can apply automatically?
[05:37] Liam: They generate a proposed configuration you can review and apply per-route. We never change runtime behavior without an explicit apply.
[05:45] [05:45 — brief crosstalk, connection noise noted: "uhh" and "sorry dropped audio"]
[05:58] Ethan: About costs — can we set hard floor/cap for spend per route?
[06:05] Maya: Yes, quotas per-route and per-team, plus alerts. We can set a monthly cap for a pilot.
[06:12] Priya: On RG latency numbers — any reference for 95th percentile for a 512-token response?
[06:18] Liam: On our verified models typical 95p for a 512-token response on an NVLink GPU pool is ~450-700ms for first chunk and then streaming token cadence of ~10-30ms per token. Big caveat: quantization and sequence length change those numbers. We'll also run a tailored test for you.
[06:40] Carlos: That sounds optimistic vs our in-house numbers. What about fallbacks to smaller models if load spikes?
[06:47] Liam: You can set waterfall fallbacks — route policy to downgrade to a cheaper, smaller model under load. Console shows the estimated change in accuracy and cost. Canary rollouts combined with fallback protect SLA.
[06:59] Priya: Security again — audit logs retention and SSO?
[07:04] Liam: SSO via SAML/OIDC supported. Audit logs retention is configurable; hosted defaults to 90 days but enterprise plans can extend. KMS integration for private deployments and HSM options for Dedicated. We'll include a short security appendix.
[07:20] Maya: Quick pause — any blockers for a pilot from your side?
[07:23] Priya: Need to check legal on data residency and then get sample prompts to match our triage. Timeline: we want a proof-of-concept within 3 weeks.
[07:32] Maya: Great. We'll aim for a POC kickoff week of Aug 31.
[07:36] [screen switches to an Optimize run showing batch recommendations]
[07:40] Liam: Demo detail — Optimize found many short prompts (avg 45 tokens) so it suggested small-batch pooling (batch size 8) with a 20ms max wait to keep latency low while benefiting from kernel efficiency. Also suggested enabling KV prefix caching for repeated task instructions but flagged it for review due to PII.
[08:05] Ethan: On prefix caching — can we selectively cache only the system instruction not the user content?
[08:10] Liam: Yup, split caching is supported. System prompt cached, user text never cached.
[08:15] Priya: If we do structured JSON output, how do we handle streaming partial JSON?
[08:20] Liam: There's a small gotcha: partial JSON streaming can yield invalid JSON mid-stream. We typically recommend either: 1) stream plain text and then parse at the end, 2) use function-calling style which gives you a single structured payload, or 3) emit newline-delimited JSON chunks. Each has tradeoffs for frontend parsing and latency.
[08:42] Carlos: Any logs/trace hooks to correlate request -> model -> downstream calls?
[08:46] Liam: Console traces every request id with per-token latency histogram and optional trace export to your tracing backend. We also have webhooks for large events.
[08:58] [08:58 — brief silence as attendees review the Console]
[09:12] Priya: Ok, last question: if we start hosted and later want to move to Private, how hard is migration of routes and configs?
[09:18] Maya: We provide an export of all route configs, model pins, and rollout states. There's an automated import into Private with a compatibility check. We've migrated a few customers — typical lift 2-4 weeks depending on network setup.
[09:32] Ethan: Good to know.
[09:36] Maya: Let's recap — action items: Liam runs latency/test using your anonymized traces; Priya/Ethan share prompts and expected QPS; Maya sends pricing and security docs. Any final questions?
[09:50] Priya: No, that's it. Thanks!
[09:53] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with notes and the deck.
[09:57] [meeting ends]
notes: Shared deck: https://redwood.example/decks/blueharbor-hosted-demo.pdf. Security appendix and SOC2 link to be sent. Customer asked for POC in 3 weeks. Some transcription noise around 00:05 and 05:45.
